previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mrs. ___ was admitted for not feeling like herself, with symptoms of shortness of breath, chest discomfort, cough, and generalized body pain. Initial concern for cardiac or pulmonary causes was ruled out with normal troponins, a non-diagnostic EKG, and a CT chest that showed no pulmonary embolus or pneumonia but revealed a small right pleural effusion and nonspecific lung changes likely related to prior radiation. She was treated for a mild asthma exacerbation or bronchitis with nebulizers, azithromycin, and continued home inhalers. Lethargy was attributed to pain and opioid use, and her MS Contin was held initially but restarted as she became more alert. Roxicet was transitioned to liquid form for easier use. Her chronic conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis and tracheal cancer history, were managed, and she was discharged home with home services, improved symptoms, and follow-up arranged with pulmonary and specialty clinics.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___,

It was a pleasure taking care of you during your hospital stay 
at ___. You were admitted because of nasal congestion, 
fatigue, abdominal pain and vomitting. You also had chest pain 
during your stay. You were tested for the flu, and this test was 
negative. It is mostly likely that you had a viral upper 
respiratory tract infection. You were hydrated, your vomiting 
stopped and you were able to slowly tolerate food. 

It is likely that your chest pain is being caused by painful 
swallowing. Because you are on steroid medication (prednisone), 
it increases your risk of developing fungal/yeast infections in 
your esophagus, which can produce pain. We started you on a 
medication called fluconazole that you should take daily for a 
total of 2 weeks. This will help get rid of fungus in your 
esophagus if it is there.  We think you got this infection 
because of steroids and antibiotics and thus it is very 
important that you only get these medications when it is 
absolutely necesssary!

You were also evaluated by our GI doctors, who recommended a 
barium swallow, which showed a narrowing of your esophagus. This 
area of the esophagus was not dilated at this time because there 
was too much inflammation. However, they also found an area of 
ulceration that also may be contributing to your pain. It is 
important that you take pantoprazole twice daily to help 
decrease the acidity of your stomach and follow-up with GI to 
find out what that biopsy showed.

Please note the following changes to your medications.
Please START:
1. Fluconazole 200mg daily for a total of 14 days. You last dose 
should be taken on ___.
2. Leflunomide - once the prior authorization goes through.
3. Pantoprazole 40mg twice daily

Please CHANGE:
1. Prednisone - take 20mg daily (instead of 40mg daily), and 
reduce the dose by 2.5mg every 7 days until you are taking 5mg 
per day. This means you should take 4 tablets daily (20mg) for 1 
day, then take 3.5 tablets (17.5mg) daily for 7 days, then take 
3 tablets (15mg) daily for 7 days, then take 2.5 tablets 
(12.5mg) daily for 7 days, then take 2 tablets (10mg) daily for 
7 days, then take 1.5 tablets (7.5mg) daily for 7 days, then 
continue to take 1 tablet (5mg) daily.

Please STOP:
1. Ranitidine (you will be taking Pantoprazole)
2. Cetirizine - this can cause drowsiness
3. Cholecalciferol - your vitamin D supplementation is included 
in the other medication you are already taking, called CALCIUM 
CARBONATE-VITAMIN D3 [CALCIUM 600 + D(3)]
4. Metoclopramide (Reglan)

No other changes were made to your medications. Please continue 
taking them as prescribed.

INDICATION:  Green productive sputum.

COMPARISON:  ___ chest radiograph and chest CTA.

UPRIGHT AP AND LATERAL VIEWS OF THE CHEST:  There are low lung volumes.  The
cardiac, mediastinal, and hilar contours appear unchanged, with the heart size
within normal limits.  The aortic knob remains calcified.  The pulmonary
vascularity is not engorged.  Linear opacities in both upper lobes reflect
areas of scarring as demonstrated on the prior CT.  No new focal areas of
consolidation are present.  No pleural effusion or pneumothorax is visualized.
There are no acute osseous abnormalities.  Left humeral head prosthesis is
partially imaged.

IMPRESSION:  No new areas of consolidation to suggest pneumonia.  Bilateral
upper lobe linear opacities compatible with areas of scarring.

CLINICAL HISTORY:  ___ woman with breast cancer and non-small cell
lung cancer, tracheal cancer diagnosed in ___ status post chemo and
radiation with complication of radiation esophagitis, now with recurrent
odynophagia.  Evaluate for stricture that may be causing odynophagia.

DOUBLE-CONTRAST UPPER GI:  There is an esophageal narrowing spanning
approximately 3 cm in the upper esophagus at the level of the aortic arch,
with hold up of contrast just above the stricture.  The maximal width of the
distended esophagus at the stricture approximately 6 mm.  Mucosal irregularity
is seen just above the stricture.  Contrast is held up just above the
stricture, which is not cleared by secondary peristaltic waves. A 12-mm barium
tablet is held up just above the stricture. 

There are normal primary peristaltic waves identified. Tertiary peristaltic
waves are also seen.

There is no gastroesophageal reflux demonstrated and no hiatal hernia.  The
stomach empties promptly and is grossly unremarkable.

After approximately 1 hour, the barium tablet is no longer seen in the upper
esophagus. It is not seen in the stomach/proximal small bowel and has likely
dissolved.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Esophageal narrowing/stricture spanning approximately 3 cm at the level of
the aortic arch with mucosal irregularity above the stricture.  A 12-mm barium
tablet is not able to traverse past the stricture.
2.  Normal primary peristaltic waves identified.  Tertiary peristaltic waves
seen.
